Introduction: CERA Medical is an SECP-registered biomedical research and development company. We test candidate treatments in animal models, in cells and by computer simulation, run the molecular laboratory work that supports those studies, analyse microbiome, omics and clinical data through to publication-ready results, and prepare the evidence reviews and technical reports on which health decisions rest.
1.1 Preclinical Studies
Tag: In Vivo, In Vitro, In Silico
Grid summary: Safety and efficacy testing in animal models, in cells and by simulation

Description: We establish whether a candidate treatment is safe and effective before it reaches human trials. Studies are run in three complementary settings: in vivo, in animal models of disease; in vitro, in cell-based systems; and in silico, by computer simulation of how a compound binds its target. A project may use one setting or move through all three, so that a compound predicted to bind its target is tested in cells and then in an animal model of the disease.
In vivo studies
Studies in animal models of disease, carried out in our Animal House.
Safety Assessment. Systematic evaluation of potential adverse effects and risk profiling
Efficacy Testing. Measurement of treatment effectiveness under controlled laboratory conditions
Toxicology Studies. Identification of toxic thresholds and dose-response relationships
Behavioural Testing. Assays of memory, anxiety-like behaviour and locomotor activity
Study Standards. Studies are designed, conducted and documented in line with the principles of Good Laboratory Practice, under a protocol approved by the institutional animal ethics committee
Available research animals: Mice, rats, rabbits and guinea pigs
In vitro studies
Cell-based models of disease, run in our Cell Culture Lab.
In-Vitro Models. Cell-based laboratory systems that replicate disease environments
Cellular Assays. Quantitative testing of cell viability, proliferation and function
Pathway Analysis. Mapping of signalling cascades and molecular disease mechanisms
Therapeutic Testing. Screening of natural products and other candidate treatments against disease models
Available cell lines: glioblastoma and other cell lines held in the Cell Culture Lab
In silico studies
Computational prediction of how a compound interacts with its protein targets, run on our GPU infrastructure.
Target Selection. Protein targets chosen from the disease pathway and prepared from published structures
Molecular Docking. Prediction of the binding site, binding pose and affinity of a compound, validated against known reference ligands
Molecular Dynamics. Simulation of the compound and its target over time to test whether the predicted complex is stable
Binding Energy Analysis. Estimation of binding free energy and of the residues that contribute most to binding
Why it matters
Preclinical testing reduces risk before human clinical trials, identifies suitable dosing strategies, generates data that can support regulatory submissions and shortens drug development timelines.
Current research

Our preclinical work is concentrated in neuroscience and oncology. Current studies centre on neuroprotection, the evaluation of antidepressant activity and social conditioning, according to the product under test. The following projects are running in our laboratories.

Methamphetamine-induced neurotoxicity. A mouse model of methamphetamine exposure in which a natural compound is tested for protective and restorative effects on recognition memory, neuroinflammation and neuronal cell death.
Social isolation stress. The effect of early-life social isolation on the brain and on behaviour, including vulnerability to drug dependence in later life.
Morphine dependence. Mouse models of morphine dependence and withdrawal, used to test candidate treatments and the signalling pathways through which they act.
Nicotine. Rodent models of nicotine exposure, in which candidate products are evaluated for their neuroprotective and behavioural effects.
Synthetic compounds in neuroscience. Newly synthesised compounds, and compounds modified from a base compound, screened for activity in neurological and behavioural models.
Gut-induced depression. Models in which disturbance of the gut microbiota produces depression-like behaviour, used to study the gut-brain axis and to test interventions.
Natural products in glioblastoma. Natural products tested against glioblastoma cell lines for their effect on cell viability and proliferation.
In silico target studies. Docking and molecular dynamics studies that test whether a compound under investigation binds the inflammatory and cell-death proteins implicated by our animal studies.

Part 2. Methodology and pipelines

Text for a "How we work" or "Methodology" page, and for the detail section of each service page. Each methodology is written as the numbered steps of a pipeline, under a one-line flow that can be drawn as a graphic.
2.1 How every project runs
Every project, whether it is a laboratory study or a data analysis, follows the same five stages.
Scoping. We discuss the research question, the material or data available and the output you need, and agree the scope, timeline and cost in writing.
Protocol. We prepare the study protocol or analysis plan before any work starts. For animal studies the protocol is approved by the institutional animal ethics committee first.
Execution. The work is carried out by the assigned scientist with the controls, replicates and quality checks defined in the protocol.
Analysis and reporting. Results are analysed with documented methods and delivered as a report with figures, tables and a methods text that can be used in a manuscript.
Follow-up. A consultation call is available on delivery, and revision rounds are included.
2.2 Preclinical studies
A. In vivo workflow
Pipeline at a glance: Study design → Model induction → Treatment → Behavioural testing → Tissue collection → Tissue analysis → Statistics and report
Step 1. Study design. Groups, sample size, doses, route and duration of treatment, endpoints and statistical analysis are fixed in a written protocol and approved by the animal ethics committee.

Step 2. Model induction. The disease state is established in the animals, for example by repeated drug exposure, by a stress procedure such as social isolation, or by disturbance of the gut microbiota.

Step 3. Treatment. The test compound is given at several dose levels alongside vehicle and disease controls. Protective designs give the compound before each exposure; restorative designs start it after the disease state is established, so that prevention and recovery can be distinguished.

Step 4. Behavioural testing. Standard assays such as the Open Field Test, the Light-Dark Box and Novel Object Recognition measure locomotor activity, anxiety-like behaviour and recognition memory. Sessions are video-recorded and scored by an automated tracking system, which removes observer bias.
Step 5. Tissue collection. Brain regions and other tissues are collected and divided for histological and molecular analysis.
Step 6. Tissue analysis. Histology (H&E, Nissl), immunohistochemistry, ELISA and biochemical assays quantify neuronal damage, inflammation, cell death and oxidative stress.
Step 7. Statistics and report. Group comparisons with the tests specified in the protocol; report with figures, raw data tables and methods text.
B. In vitro workflow
Pipeline at a glance: Model set-up → Treatment → Cellular assays → Mechanism → Analysis and report
Step 1. Model set-up. The cell line relevant to the disease is cultured under standard conditions and checked before use.
Step 2. Treatment. Cells are exposed to the test material across a range of concentrations and time points, with untreated, vehicle and reference controls.
Step 3. Cellular assays. Cell viability, proliferation and function are measured quantitatively
Step 4. Mechanism. Signalling pathways affected by the treatment are examined at gene and protein level.
Step 5. Analysis and report. Dose-response analysis with replicate experiments; report with figures and methods text.
C. In silico pipeline
The same pipeline is applied to any compound and any set of protein targets.
Pipeline at a glance: Target selection → Ligand preparation → Molecular docking → Pose inspection → Molecular dynamics → Trajectory analysis → Binding free energy → Report

Step 1. Target selection. Protein targets are chosen from the disease pathway and the literature; three-dimensional structures are retrieved and repaired where residues or side chains are missing. Tools: RCSB Protein Data Bank, PDBFixer. Output: Prepared target structures.
Step 2. Ligand preparation. The compound structure is retrieved or drawn, converted to three dimensions and energy-minimised. Tools: PubChem, Open Babel. Output: Prepared ligand files.

Step 3. Molecular docking. The compound is docked into the defined binding site of each target. The set-up is validated by redocking the co-crystallised ligand and by docking known reference inhibitors as positive controls. Tools: AutoDock Vina. Output: Binding poses and affinities.
Step 4. Pose inspection. Each pose is checked for steric clashes, hydrogen bonds and contacts with the residues known to matter for binding. Tools: Structure visualisation. Output: Interaction maps.

Step 5. Molecular dynamics. Each complex is solvated, neutralised at physiological salt concentration, minimised and equilibrated, then simulated for 100 ns in replicate on GPU. Tools: GROMACS, AmberTools. Output: Trajectories.

Step 6. Trajectory analysis. Stability and flexibility of the complex (RMSD, RMSF, radius of gyration, solvent-accessible surface), hydrogen bond occupancy, clustering, principal component analysis and free energy landscape. Tools: GROMACS, MDAnalysis. Output: Stability plots and tables.
Step 7. Binding free energy. Binding free energy with decomposition into the contribution of each residue. Tools: gmx_MMPBSA. Output: Energy tables.
Step 8. Report. Publication-ready figures, tables and a methods text; replicates are reported individually. Tools: Python. Output: Report and figure files.
2.3 Molecular research

Samples are logged on receipt and stored under the conditions the assay requires. Genomic variants are characterised by PCR and Sanger sequencing in our Genomics Lab. Gene expression is measured by RT-PCR with reference genes and no-template controls, and protein expression by Western blot and ELISA with standards and replicate wells. Biochemical assays quantify biomarkers in tissue, serum and cell samples. Tissue for histopathology is processed, sectioned and stained with H&E or Nissl stain, or labelled by immunohistochemistry, then imaged in our Microscopy Lab and quantified. Where no suitable method exists, we develop and validate one and deliver the protocol with its performance data. Instruments, kits and assay platforms are made available as per project requirements.
2.4 Metagenomic data analysis

We provide validated reference pipelines that can be customised by adding or removing analytical tools to match the requirements of your project. Three workflows cover most studies: read-based profiling of shotgun metagenomes, genome-resolved analysis that recovers metagenome-assembled genomes, and amplicon analysis of 16S or ITS marker genes.
A. Shotgun metagenomes: read-based profiling

Pipeline at a glance: Data retrieval → Quality control → Taxonomic classification → Functional annotation → Diversity analysis → AMR and virulence screening → Statistical analysis → Report and delivery

Step 1. Data retrieval. Raw FASTQ or FASTA files are downloaded from the sequencing provider's server, a secure link or a public repository by accession number, and checked against the sample metadata. Tools: Secure transfer, SRA Toolkit. Output: Confirmed sample sheet.
Step 2. Quality control. Adapter trimming, quality filtering and removal of host reads. Tools: FastQC, fastp, KneadData. Output: QC report, clean reads.

Step 3. Taxonomic classification. Species-level identification and relative abundance estimation at every taxonomic rank. Tools: Kraken2, Bracken, MetaPhlAn 4. Output: Taxonomy tables, abundance plots.
Step 4. Functional annotation. Gene family and pathway profiling; GO term and metabolic mapping. Tools: HUMAnN 3, eggNOG, KEGG. Output: Pathway and gene family tables.
Step 5. Diversity analysis. Alpha and beta diversity; PCoA and other ordinations. Tools: QIIME 2, vegan (R). Output: Diversity plots, PCoA.
Step 6. AMR and virulence screening. Detection of resistance genes and virulence factors in assembled contigs. Tools: CARD/RGI, VFDB, ABRicate. Output: Resistance and virulence gene tables.
Step 7. Statistical analysis. Differential abundance, biomarker discovery and multivariate modelling. Tools: LEfSe, DESeq2, MaAsLin2. Output: Differential abundance results.

Step 8. Report and delivery. Publication-ready figures, a PDF report with a written description of the results, and all result files, within 3 weeks. Tools: R Markdown, ggplot2, Python. Output: PDF report, figures (PNG/SVG), data files.
B. Shotgun metagenomes: genome-resolved analysis (MAG recovery)

Where the study needs genomes and not only taxonomic profiles, clean reads are assembled and binned into metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), which allows strain-level comparison, detection of candidate novel species and gene-level annotation.
Pipeline at a glance: Assembly → Assembly QC → Coverage and binning → Bin quality → Dereplication → Taxonomy → Annotation → Abundance and association
C. 16S and ITS amplicon sequencing
Pipeline at a glance: Read QC → Denoising → Taxonomy → Data integration → Diversity analysis → Differential abundance → Functional prediction
Functional prediction. Optional prediction of functional potential from marker genes
Analytical standards
The same rules apply to every analysis we deliver.
Every number in the report is produced by the pipeline and can be traced to an output file.
The methods text states each tool with its version and the parameters used.
The number of samples retained at each stage is reported, with the reason for any sample that was excluded.
Sequencing run, lane and other batch structure are carried into the statistical models.
Covariates that differ between study groups, such as age, are examined and adjusted for.
Scripts and intermediate files are delivered with the report, so that the analysis can be reproduced.
What you receive
Quality control. QC report and clean reads
Taxonomic profiling. Taxonomy tables and abundance plots
Functional analysis. Pathway and gene family tables
Diversity analysis. Alpha and beta diversity plots and PCoA
Statistical analysis. Differential abundance results
Final report. PDF report with a written description of the results, and all data files
All result files, figures (PNG and SVG) and a full PDF report are included. Revisions continue until the analysis is complete, and a consultation call is available on delivery.
2.5 Biomedical and omics data analysis
Pipeline at a glance: Scoping → Data intake and audit → Cleaning and quality control → Processing and annotation → Statistical analysis and modelling → Validation → Report and revisions
2.6 Evidence synthesis and technical reports
Pipeline at a glance: Question and protocol → Literature search → Screening → Data extraction and appraisal → Synthesis and analysis → Report writing → Review and delivery

Page title: Privacy Terms
Effective date: [date of publication]
1. Who we are

CERA Medical [SMC PVT LTD] is a biomedical research and development company registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan. Our office is on the 2nd Floor, BIC, C2 Building, Pak-Austria Fachhochschule: Institute of Applied Sciences and Technology (PAF-IAST), Mang, Haripur, Pakistan. We develop natural healthcare products and provide research services: preclinical studies, molecular research, metagenomic data analysis, biomedical and omics data analysis, and evidence synthesis and technical reporting. In these terms, "CERA Medical", "we" and "us" refer to this company, which is responsible for the personal information described below.
2. What these terms cover

These terms explain what information we collect through www.ceramed.org and in the course of providing our services, how we use and protect it, how long we keep it, and the choices available to you. They apply to visitors to the website, to people who contact us, and to clients who request a service.
3. Information we collect
Information you give us. When you contact us or request a service, we collect your name, email address, telephone number, institution, country and the content of your message.

Service files and materials. To carry out a service, we receive the files and materials you send us or ask us to retrieve. These may include sequencing data, sample metadata, health, survey and programme datasets, draft reports and manuscripts, figures and tables, test compounds and biological samples together with their accompanying records.
Billing information. We keep the name and address used for invoicing and a record of payments received. [Card details are processed by our payment provider and are not stored by CERA Medical.]
Orders. [When you buy a product from us, we collect your delivery address and keep a record of the order.]
Information collected automatically. Our servers record your IP address, browser and device type, the pages you visit and the date and time of each visit. Cookies are described in section 11.
4. How we use information
We use the information described above for the following purposes:
to respond to enquiries and prepare quotations;
to carry out the service requested and deliver its results;
to issue invoices, receive payment and keep the accounting records that the law requires;
to maintain the security and performance of the website;
to send messages about a service in progress and, where you have agreed, news about our services and products;
to comply with legal obligations and respond to lawful requests from competent authorities.

We process information on the basis of your consent, the need to perform a service you have requested, our legitimate interest in operating and securing our services, and the legal obligations that apply to us.
5. Research data, health data and samples

Files, datasets, samples and compounds submitted for a service remain the property of the client, and the client retains full ownership of the data and results generated from them. We use them only on the client's instructions and only for the service requested. We do not use client data or materials for our own research, publications, product development or marketing, and we do not disclose them to other clients. Where a project is carried out as a research collaboration, ownership, publication and authorship are set out in a separate written agreement.

Our services are designed for de-identified data and coded samples. We ask clients not to send information that directly identifies study participants, survey respondents, patients or donors, and the client remains responsible for the ethical approval and consent that govern the underlying study or programme. We do not attempt to identify any individual from sequencing data, health data, samples or metadata. Where sequencing reads from human samples contain human genetic material, we remove those reads during quality control and do not analyse them for any other purpose. If we receive files or samples that carry direct identifiers without prior agreement, we inform the client and return or delete them.

Where a client organisation requires it, we sign a data sharing or data protection agreement before any data are transferred and follow that organisation's data protection requirements, including its rules on data about children. Results are reported in aggregate, and small groups are suppressed so that no individual can be identified from a report.

Every member of staff and every contracted specialist who has access to client files or materials is bound by a duty of confidentiality. A non-disclosure agreement is available on request before any file or sample is transferred.
6. Who we share information with
We do not sell personal information. We share it only in the following circumstances:
with staff and contracted specialists who need it to deliver the service, under obligations of confidentiality;

with providers that support our operations, namely website hosting, email, secure file storage and transfer, and payment processing, under terms that limit their use of the information to the service they provide to us;
with a person you name, for example a co-author or collaborator, when you instruct us to do so;
where disclosure is required by law, by a court order or by a competent authority.
7. Where information is stored

Information is stored on [systems located in Pakistan. Some of the providers listed in section 6 may hold information on servers outside Pakistan. Where that is the case, we take reasonable steps to ensure that the information receives a comparable level of protection.
8. Security

Access to client information and materials is restricted to the personnel assigned to the service. [Files are transferred over encrypted connections, stored on password-protected systems and backed up regularly.] No method of transmission or storage is completely secure. If a security incident occurs that is likely to affect you, we will inform you without undue delay and explain the steps we are taking.
9. How long we keep information

We keep information only for as long as it is needed for the purposes set out in these terms. The periods that apply to each category, and the way information and materials are deleted or destroyed at the end of each period, are set out in our Data Retention Policy.
10. Your choices and rights

You may ask us at any time to confirm what information we hold about you, to provide a copy of it, to correct it, or to delete it. You may also withdraw a consent you have given and ask us to stop sending updates. To make a request, write to medicalcera@gmail.com. We respond within 30 days. We may need to verify your identity before acting on a request, and we may retain information that the law requires us to keep.
11. Cookies

The website uses cookies that are necessary for it to work.You can accept or reject non-essential cookies in the banner shown on your first visit and change your choice at any time in Cookie Settings. You can also block or delete cookies in your browser, although parts of the site may then not work as intended.
12. Children

The website and our services are intended for researchers, professionals, organisations and adult consumers. We do not knowingly collect personal information from anyone under 18 years of age through the website. Research and programme datasets that concern children are handled only in de-identified form, as described in section 5.
13. Links to other websites
The website may link to journals, databases and other external sites. We are not responsible for the content or privacy practices of those sites and recommend reading their own terms.
14. Changes to these terms

We may revise these terms when our services or the applicable law change. The effective date at the top of the page shows when the current version was published. Where a change materially affects information we already hold about clients, we will notify them by email.
15. Contact
Questions about these terms and requests concerning your information may be sent to CERA Medical, 2nd Floor, BIC, C2 Building, PAF-IAST, Mang, Haripur, Pakistan, by email to medicalcera@gmail.com.

1. Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how long CERA Medical keeps the information and materials it receives through its website and services, and what happens to them at the end of each period. It applies to information held in any format, including files on our servers, cloud storage, email accounts, portable drives and backups, and to physical samples, test compounds and laboratory records.
2. Principles

We keep information and materials only for as long as they serve the purpose for which they were received or for as long as the law requires. Client data and samples are held for the shortest practical period after delivery, so that we can answer questions and make revisions, and are then deleted, returned or destroyed. Where a data sharing agreement with a client sets a different period, that agreement prevails. Clients are advised to keep their own copies of all files and reserve samples, since CERA Medical does not act as an archive.
3. Retention schedule
Enquiries that do not lead to a service. Retention: [12 months] from the last correspondence. At the end: Deleted from the mailbox and form records.

Client contact details and service correspondence. Retention: For the duration of the client relationship and [2 years] after the last completed service. At the end: Deleted, except where they form part of an accounting record.

Raw sequencing data and sample metadata. Retention: [90 days] after delivery of the final report, or longer at the client's written request while a manuscript is in preparation or under review. At the end: Securely deleted from all working storage.
Analysis outputs, reports, figures, scripts and simulation files. Retention: [12 months] after delivery, to support revisions and reviewer queries. At the end: Securely deleted.

Health, clinical, survey and programme datasets. Retention: [30 days] after the client accepts the final report, or the period set in the data sharing agreement. At the end: Returned to the client or securely deleted, with written confirmation.
Draft reports, manuscripts and related documents. Retention: [6 months] after delivery of the final version. At the end: Securely deleted.

Client samples and test compounds. Retention: [30 days] after delivery of the final report. At the end: Returned at the client's request and cost, or destroyed under our biosafety and chemical waste procedures.
Tissue blocks, slides and other material generated in a study. Retention: [12 months] after delivery of the final report. At the end: Returned at the client's request, or destroyed.

Laboratory study records: protocols, raw data, notebooks, behavioural recordings and instrument files. Retention: [ 3 months ] after delivery of the final report, so that results can be verified. At the end: Securely deleted or destroyed, or transferred to the client on request.
Invoices, payment records and other accounting documents. Retention: 6 years after the end of the tax year to which they relate, as required by tax law. At the end: Deleted or destroyed.
[Product orders and delivery details] Retention: [1 years, as part of the accounting record]. At the end: [Deleted or destroyed].
Mailing list for updates. Retention: Until the subscriber unsubscribes. At the end: Removed from the list; a record of the unsubscribe request is kept so that no further messages are sent.
Records of consent given through forms. Retention: For as long as the related information is held and [3 years] afterwards. At the end: Deleted.
Website server logs. Retention: [90 days]. At the end: Overwritten automatically.
[Analytics data] Retention: [14 months, or the period set in the analytics tool]. At the end: [Deleted automatically].
Backups. Retention: [30 days] after deletion from live systems. At the end: Overwritten in the normal backup cycle.
4. Deletion on request

A client may ask us to delete submitted files, or to return or destroy submitted materials, before the end of the scheduled period by writing to medicalcera@gmail.com. We act on the request within [14 days] and confirm in writing that this has been done. Accounting records are not affected by such a request, because the law requires us to keep them.
5. Longer retention

Information and materials are kept beyond the scheduled period only in three situations: where the client has asked us in writing to keep project files or samples for longer, for example while a manuscript is under review; where the law, a regulator or an ethics committee requires it; and where they are needed to resolve a dispute or a complaint. In each case they are deleted or destroyed once the reason for keeping them has ended.
6. How information and materials are destroyed

Electronic files are deleted from working storage, cloud folders, email attachments and any portable drive used for transfer, and are removed from backups in the normal backup cycle. Storage media are wiped before reuse or disposal. Paper records are shredded. Biological samples and test compounds are destroyed under the laboratory's biosafety and chemical waste procedures. [The date of deletion or destruction is recorded in the project file.]
7. Responsibility and review

CEO is responsible for applying this policy and for checking each quarter that files and materials due for deletion have been removed. The policy is reviewed once a year and whenever our services or the applicable law change.
